chapters.html:
Phainon looks upon Mydei and his chest aches with a hunger his mother says he is not supposed to feel.

Mydei lays in the warm grass, his golden hair blending in with the heather, and his eyes closed as he naps under the hot summer sun. His head is pillowed on his abandoned shirt, and Phainon cannot look away from the honeyed expanse of Mydei’s bare skin.

Mydei is so beautiful. He’s as beautiful as Kephale’s most lovingly crafted angel—an angel that dove from heaven to become the embodiment of the sun itself. 

Aquila.

Mydei is Phainon’s Aquila, his worst temptation, and Mydei doesn’t even know.

Mydei is laying in the grass, naked from the waist up, because they are two young men who are best friends. Mydei is just soaking up the summer sun warming him up until sweat shines in the light. 

“Are you going to keep staring, Phainon? I’m sure a picture will last longer.”

Phainon’s cheeks color pink, but he can pass it off as a side effect of the hot sun. He hadn’t realized that Mydei opened his eyes. Phainon flops onto his back instead of facing the heavy gaze Mydei gives him. 

“I wasn’t staring,” Phainon petulantly defends himself, though it takes great effort to manage it.

”Admiring, then.”

Phainon sucks his teeth. He hasn’t shed his own shirt and his buttoned up polo feels suffocating. His sweat has it sticking to his skin, and Phainon so badly wants to take it off to cool down. They’re both young men; being half-naked together is totally normal. No one would care if they were found out. 

But the thought of being even half-naked with Mydei makes something stir and flutter inside of Phainon’s stomach.

That might be normal, expected in the summer heat, but Phainon isn’t sure that he knows what he feels is.

”Will the sun affect your tattoos?” Phainon asks instead of lingering, trying to turn the conversation away from his traitorous gaze. “I thought that it was bad for color tattoos to be exposed to the sun for an extended period of time.”

”They’re not exactly fresh,” Mydei says, “and I have sunscreen on.”

Mydei says something else that is lost to the intense buzzing in Phainon’s ears. He is caught up by the thought of Mydei rubbing smooth and wet sunscreen on his bare muscles, careful that every inch of his skin is covered and that his tattoos—tattoos that go so far down Mydei’s torso that they disappear down his basketball shorts before reappearing on his thighs—are as safe from sun damage as the rest of them.

Did Mydei stop at only one layer of sunscreen, or did he add another before he met Phainon in the courtyard.

Phainon’s thoughts are out of hand. He might need to go to confession again.

(“Father, I have experienced lust several times this week. I have thought about the body of another man in ways I should not have. I repent, Father, and I seek to absolve myself from this sin.”

Does their local priest grow tired of Phainon’s pathetic confessions? He hears his shame every week and assigns him any number of  ‘Our Father’s  and ‘Hail Mnestia’s, and a day of fasting in these trying times—surely he wishes that Phainon would just wake up with a normal attraction to, say, Castorice or even Cyrene, despite the latter’s affinity for the occult.

They are young women. They are lovely and soft.

They are nothing like Mydeimos, with his muscles, sharp edges, and tattoos.)

”Do you need some more? To keep them safe, I mean,” Phainon finally asks. He is resolutely not looking at Mydei and is instead trying to discern shapes in the clouds lazily crawling above them. 

“Nah,” Mydei’s voice is soft and Phainon takes a glance at him. “Not yet, at least.”

They hold each other’s gaze for a while, and Phainon observes Mydei and lets himself be admired in turn. 

How many times have they looked at each other like this?

Phainon sees a drop of sweat fall down Mydei’s throat and swallows thickly. 

Mydei is bright and beautiful. He is a bringer of light—just like Aquila before the madness.

”You’re awfully quiet today,” Mydei says, breaking their tense silence. “Is it the heat? Should we go back inside?”

“Not much to say,” Phainon replies, soft and careful. “I’m okay. I want to stay out for a while longer.”

”Okay. Come closer, tell me the stories about what you see in the clouds.” Mydei knows Phainon well.

And Phainon, never one to deny Mydei, does just that. He weaves a story about a yawning dragon, a dancing thief, a knight, and a noble prince. They meet a priestess who tells them of a prophecy, and together, they save the kingdom.

It’s a happy story. 

(“The prince marries—“

“No one,” Mydei cuts Phainon off, shaking his head. “He lives in peaceful, loving company with his knight.” Mydei pauses. “For they are the best of friends—or so history will say.”

Phainon isn’t sure what to say to that, but he decides he agrees. The prince and his knight. The knight and his prince.

A happily ever after, indeed.)

”We should catch frogs. Whoever catches the most frogs wins,” Phainon says in lieu of telling another story. “And then we can go to the market to get some dinner?”

“You want to catch frogs? Are we boys or men, Phainon?”

“Out here there are none of those rules—we are neither boys nor men! We are merely Mydei and Phainon, and we can do as we please!”

As cheerful as Phainon’s words are, they feel like sand in his mouth. He claims that no rules apply to them here, that society is of little consequence to them, but he lets his fear of judgement keep him from crossing the only line left between himself and Mydei because they are still men. 

They are done growing out of their awkward, gangly limbs of boyhood, and that means that while the knight and prince may live together as fond friends in Phainon’s pretty story, Mydei and Phainon can only be that: friends.

They cannot turn to each other, hands calloused from their boyish games and war, and embrace as lovers.

They can’t.

…Can they?

The fears that Phainon feels from holding onto society’s rules should not apply here because society can’t even find them, so why does Phainon hold onto them so tightly?

(Because Phainon is a coward. A goddamn coward who is terrified of being as free as he wants to be.)

Mydei is looking at him, his eyes soft and concern knitting his handsome brow. He’s so beautiful and so close to Phainon. 

“We can catch frogs if you want, Phainon, but you have to answer a question for me first—can you do that?”

Dread constricts Phainon’s throat. He can say ‘no’ and Mydei wouldn’t punish him for that. Phainon could also lie, but Phainon doesn’t want to lie to Mydei.

What’s the thing that people say? That the truth can set you free?

”Of course,” Phainon says, grinning with a confidence that he cannot feel, “do your worst!”

”Are you into me?”

So lightly said. So nonchalant. 

Phainon wishes that he could be like that about anything, let alone asking if his best friend was into him and found him attractive.

”Are you asking if I’m gay?” Good. Phainon’s voice doesn’t shake. 

“I’m asking if you like men, which is not the same thing as ‘are you gay?’ Besides, I’m pretty sure my question was clear and concise: are you into me, Phainon?”

Yes, by Sky Father Kephale, yes, Phainon is hopelessly into Mydei. Does that mean that Phainon is gay? Does it mean that Phainon is only attracted to men when it comes to Mydei?

(‘Like’ doesn’t feel a strong enough word, but the stronger word is too terrifying for Phainon to consider. )

”I’m…” Phainon swallows thickly. “Mydeimos, I’m not supposed to.” Phainon’s voice is shaking now and his eyes start to sting in…

In what? Frustration? Shame? A mix of both or neither?

”Phainon, that’s not a ‘no’. You don’t need to answer me at all, I shouldn’t have put you on the spot like that,” Mydei says with a voice so soft and tender that the vice grip it has on Phainon’s heart is entirely justified as he reaches a hand into the empty space between the two of them. “I’m sorry. We can forget about it entirely.”

They could. Phainon should take this graciously offered out and maybe they can pretend that nothing ever happened. Phainon and Mydei can remain the best of friends, to be the best man in each other’s weddings to pretty women, to be the godfathers to each other’s children. 

But, despite his doubts, despite his shame, Phainon doesn’t just want to be the best friend, the best man, the godfather. Phainon does want to be Mydei’s best friend, but he doesn’t want to be anything other than the man standing across from Mydei at the altar as his to-be-husband, and the father to any children in the future. 

“I-If…” Phainon winces as his voice cracks and he swallows the lump in his throat to try again. “If I was into you, what does that mean for us, Mydei? We can’t just…”

“We can, Phainon. All you need to do is be selfish for the first time in your life.

Selfish…

Phainon has never tried being selfish. He’s been a happy people-pleaser all his life—the church youth group leader, the altar boy, the boy scout. Nothing but helpful. Nothing but good.

Perhaps, Phainon thinks as he meets Mydei’s beautiful, golden gaze, it is time for the golden boy to let himself be tarnished. Being bad has always been one of Phainon’s greatest fears, but Mydei gives him the courage to step forward and try and conquer that fear.

”Is lust one of the seven deadly sins?” Phainon asks, his voice barely above a whisper. He knows the answer, but he wants Mydei’s answer. 

”You’d know better than I would,” Mydei answers. He shifts closer to Phainon, shrinking the distance between them a little bit more. “I don’t think that it should be. Have you ever gone to confession about feeling lust, Phainon?”

”Many times,” Phainon easily admits. “But… It can’t be that bad of a sin, can it? How else can children be conceived?”

”They’re not conceived. They’re brought by the stork.” Flat, but full of amusement. Mydei is just teasing him and that eases a little more of Phainon’s shame-enforced walls down. 

“But,” Mydei adds. He brings a strong, calloused hand to Phainon’s cheek, knuckles brushing tentatively over his cheekbone. “I don’t think that lust is the worst of the deadly sins. It’s not actually particularly deadly, is it?”

It’s not. It’s honestly far from being deadly. 

“It’s not. Mydeimos, I— I am attracted to you. I want you, I lust after you, and,” Phainon takes a deep breath, refusing to break Mydei’s gaze as he leans into the brush of his hand, “I am tired of being ashamed of it.”

Mydei’s answering smile is soft and even more tension releases from Phainon’s shoulders.

“You know,” Mydei whispers, leaning in to brush his arched nose against Phainon’s. It is tender and intimate, and Phainon’s heart leaps in his chest.

They have never been this close before. It is so overwhelming, so different, but oh, is Phainon obsessed with this change. He wants more, but he isn’t sure that he knows how to ask for it.

”There is more to sexuality than just liking men or just likely women. You can like both—I do.”

Oh.

This isn’t a set up—not that Phainon really thought it was—and Phainon swallows thickly.

”You do?”

”Mhm. You can, too, if that feels right for you. Nothing wrong with that.” Mydei sounds so sure of himself that Phainon can’t find it in him to disagree. “Would you like to kiss me to find out?”

A kiss?

Phainon never thought that a kiss between himself and Mydei was an option. But now that he knows that it is, he can’t manage to deny himself the opportunity. 

Phainon can verbally agree, but he fears that any more hesitation will take the nerves he’s built up. He surges forward with clumsy eagerness, smushing their noses together at first before their lips finally meet.

Mydei makes a noise—of surprise or discomfort, Phainon isn’t sure—against Phainon’s mouth, and he cradles Phainon’s face in both hands to hold his head still. He takes charge of the kiss, tongue gently prodding at the seam of Phainon’s lips.

Phainon has kissed people before, but never with tongue, and his head swims with the foreign sensation of not only kissing Mydei, but kissing Mydei with tongue…

It should probably feel wrong; the way the church and the miserable old folk talked about the consequences of kissing the same gender, Phainon had almost expected the earth to open up beneath them and swallow them both whole for their united sin. 

Instead, the kiss feels like deliverance. Mydei presses his body against Phainon’s as he rolls Phainon onto his back, keeping him firmly pressed into the summer-warmed grass. It is so perfect that their mutual attraction can’t possibly be wrong in the grand scheme of things. 

If Kephale wants all of his children to be happy, doesn’t he? If so, what would he want to punish a love such as theirs?

Phainon’s hands map out the red tattoos on Mydei’s torso, cultural markings of the faith of Castrum Kremnos. Nikador doesn’t punish a relationship like theirs, like Kephale allegedly does. The Kremnoan faith is so different and yet so lovely.

Phainon breaks their kiss, one hand leaving Mydei’s shoulder to instead cradle his cheek. His hand trembles, but Phainon feels steadier than he ever has in his adult life. This is their safe space, a place where no one can find them and make them feel bad for their feelings. 

“Mydeimos…”

“Too much?” Mydei asks, biting his lower lip. His flushed cheeks are beautiful, and Phainon wants nothing more than to kiss Mydei again. And again. And again.

”No, no… It was perfect, Mydeimos. I just… I never expected something like this to happen today. I thought we would just…”

”And are you sorry we…?”

It is not like Mydei to be hesitant, and Phainon hates seeing it. He needs to put an end to it. 

“No! No, Mydei… I am sure of nothing but how I feel about you at this moment. I could never regret this, never regret you.”

Phainon can see relief in the slump of Mydei’s shoulders and he rubs gentle curses in Mydei’s strong cheekbone. This moment is the most beautiful moment in Phainon’s life and he doesn’t know what will happen in the future, but if he can hold onto this moment and Mydei, he can face the world at large.

”You are so… One day, you and I will leave this small town. We can go back to Castrum Kremnos, and…”

”And?” Phainon prompts, breathless and eager.

”Marry, if you want to. Go to school there, for sure, but we can do anything you want so long as we get away from this small town with small minded people.”

Phainon’s heart soars and he presses his forehead to Mydei’s with a shy smile. 

“Until then?”

”Until then, we seek our freedom here, where no one can find us. Where we can travel the world and the stories you tell within each other’s lips.”
